client: It's been really hard since my grandma passed away last month. I went to a family dinner last weekend and just couldn't handle it - everyone was trying to act normal but her chair was empty and I kept expecting to hear her laugh. I'm not sure talking about it will help when nothing can bring her back.
therapist: I hear how painful this loss is for you, and how seeing that empty chair made her absence feel so deeply real. It makes sense that you'd expect to hear her laugh in those familiar family moments—she was such an important presence in your life. What comes up for you when you notice yourself waiting to hear her voice?

client: It's like I forget for a second that she's gone, and then it hits me all over again. I feel this heavy ache in my chest and start wondering if I should have visited her more often in her last months. The guilt mixes with the sadness and makes it even harder.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying both the weight of grief and these thoughts about what you "should" have done differently, which can feel overwhelming. When those guilty thoughts arise, do you notice any other moments where you showed up for her in ways that mattered?

client: I did visit pretty regularly until COVID hit - then the nursing home had those strict rules. But I used to bring her favorite lemon cookies and we'd watch her old game shows together. I just keep thinking about how frustrated she got those last few weeks when she couldn't remember things... maybe I should have been more patient with her.
therapist: It sounds like you showed her so much love through those visits, cookies, and shared moments watching game shows—those were meaningful ways of being present for her. I'm hearing both your care for her and this painful focus on the more difficult final weeks—what do you think she would say about how you showed up for her over all those years?

client: She'd probably say I was one of the few who kept visiting regularly, even when she started repeating stories. But it's hard to hold onto that when the last memories are so fresh - her getting confused and me losing my patience sometimes. I don't know how to make peace with those final weeks being part of the story too.
therapist: It's understandable that those recent difficult memories feel so vivid right now—grief has a way of magnifying our perceived shortcomings. What would it feel like to hold both truths—that you were consistently there for her *and* that those final weeks were challenging for you both?

client: I guess it feels... complicated. Part of me knows she'd understand that frustration came from caring, not indifference. But another part keeps replaying those moments wishing I'd just smiled through it all. It's like I'm stuck between knowing I was a good grandson and feeling like I failed her at the end.
therapist: What a thoughtful reflection—it sounds like you're holding space for both the love you showed her and the very human struggle of those final weeks. I wonder if your grandma, who clearly knew your love so well, might have wanted you to extend the same compassion to yourself that you always tried to show her?

client: That makes me tear up a little, because she was always telling me not to be so hard on myself. But it's easier to believe she deserves compassion than to believe I do, if that makes sense. Maybe that's something I need to work on, but it feels wrong to go easier on myself when I could have been better for her.
therapist: It sounds like your grandma knew this tendency in you—to extend kindness more easily to others than to yourself—and that makes this pattern feel even more meaningful to recognize now. What would it feel like to honor her wisdom by trying, even in small moments, to treat yourself with the same understanding she wanted for you?

client: It feels really vulnerable to even consider that idea. Like if I go easier on myself, it somehow means I'm excusing what I did wrong. But I also remember how she'd squeeze my hand when I'd get down on myself... God, I miss that. It's just hard to imagine doing that for myself when she's not here to do it anymore.
therapist: That hand squeeze was her way of reminding you that growth and self-compassion don't erase our mistakes—they help us learn from them with love. As you miss her physical presence, what would it feel like to imagine offering yourself that same reassuring squeeze when the guilt feels heaviest?

client: It feels strange but... maybe comforting too, to imagine that. I tried pressing my own hand earlier when I was missing her, but it just made me cry harder. Maybe I'm not ready yet, or maybe I'm doing it wrong. It's easier to hold onto the guilt than to let myself feel how much I miss her.
therapist: Those tears show how deeply you loved her—sometimes grief feels overwhelming because the love was so big. There's no "wrong" way to grieve or to reach for comfort, even if it feels tender at first—what would it feel like to hold space for both the tears and the possibility of comfort, letting them coexist?

client: It feels like there's this huge knot in my chest that's part sadness and part love, but I'm scared that if I loosen it at all, the whole thing will unravel and I'll just be a mess. At the same time... I think she'd be the first to tell me it's okay to be a mess sometimes. That actually makes me smile through the tears a little.
therapist: How beautiful that even in your grief, her wisdom finds its way through—reminding you that being a mess is part of being human, just as she always knew. That mix of tears and smiles tells me your love for her is alive in you—how might it feel to let the knot loosen just enough to make space for both?

client: It feels scary but... maybe possible in tiny moments. Like when I'm making tea and remember how she'd always burn the toast, and instead of beating myself up for laughing, I let myself miss her in that happy-sad way. But I'm still not sure how to do this when the heavier guilt comes up.
therapist: What a meaningful step—noticing those small moments where memory brings both joy and sadness, and letting them coexist. When the heavier guilt arises, what would it feel like to imagine your grandma's voice reminding you that love includes imperfections—both hers and yours?
